lesson.child_mission: Prepare a clean final narrative for a real reader and explain presentation choices.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Keep the independent response and two written check responses; record oral retelling or performance where required by the task.
lesson.extension: Create a new example using a completely different character or setting, show the same skill, then explain to another person how you checked its accuracy.
lesson.guided_practice:
WE DO — attempt each prompt before comparing to the feedback.
1. Choose a title for a story about a missing bicycle and explain why it fits.
COMPARE: "The Bicycle at the Creek" suggests setting and problem better than "My Work".
2. Mark where a new paragraph should start in a three-event search story.
COMPARE: A shift to a new place or time is a common paragraph break.
3. List three proofreading checks you will use before publishing.
COMPARE: Capitals, end marks and whether every sentence is complete are useful checks.
4. Write one sentence explaining a revision you made for a reader.
COMPARE: The note should name a specific change, not only "I improved it."
lesson.independent_task:
YOU DO — complete the following substantial original task, not a copied model.
Publish a 150–250 word original narrative with a title and paragraphs. Add a short author's note identifying two revisions and one response to possible reader feedback.
lesson.learning_intention: Prepare a clean final narrative for a real reader and explain presentation choices.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper to copy only the original independent prompt; have the child respond in writing or orally as required. Save a photograph or brief parent observation for the learning record.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Publish a 150–250 word original narrative with a title and paragraphs. Add a short author's note identifying two revisions and one response to possible reader feedback. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using title on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample error: A vague title does not help a reader know what the piece is about.. Correction: "The Bicycle at the Creek" suggests setting and problem better than "My Work".. Why it helps the audience is stated.

Parent: Likely misconception: A vague title does not help a reader know what the piece is about. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating title on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with title, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about title with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for title. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.example:
WATCH MY THINKING
I change "Story" to "The Lost Lantern" so a reader anticipates a missing light and a search.

YOUR SMALL TRY
Choose a title for a story about a missing bicycle and explain why it fits.

COMPARE AND CORRECT
"The Bicycle at the Creek" suggests setting and problem better than "My Work".
teach_steps.explain:
A useful title hints at character, setting or problem without spoiling every event.

A useful title hints at character, setting or problem without spoiling every event. This matters because a reader or listener can only understand your ideas when you notice how the language works, test your understanding on specific examples and explain the evidence for your choice. Keep the meaning of the original text rather than changing facts to make an answer sound impressive. Read the model closely: which particular word, event or detail changes the meaning? Try explaining the same decision to someone else without repeating the model sentence. Then compare your new attempt with the feedback and revise anything that does not fit the actual evidence.
teach_steps.notice:
WATCH OUT
A vague title does not help a reader know what the piece is about. Re-read the prompt and correct the misunderstanding before moving on.
